outcome: The problem (Erdős Problem #7: does a distinct covering system with all moduli odd exist?) remains open. The most substantive event in the window is a May 2026 claimed proof of nonexistence submitted to the erdosproblems.com forum by user 'jinooklee' together with the AI theorem-proving system Aristotle (Harmonic), backed by a Lean 4 formalization reportedly passing an 'Aristotle verification system' audit; a fatal flaw in the formalization (a false axiom, acknowledged by the submitter) was found within days and the claim was withdrawn. Separately, a self-published Zenodo cluster by 'Giovanni Esposito' (no known affiliation, no peer review) also claims full unconditional resolution, but shows strong hallmarks of AI-generated pseudo-mathematics (invented jargon like 'arithmetic renormalization', 'Coverage Fraction βₑ', 'obstruction energy' applied to elementary number theory) and has not been reviewed or endorsed by any expert; erdosproblems.com continues to list the problem as open as of its most recent update. A distinct, modest, genuinely AI-assisted contribution also appeared: Mian & Siddique (arXiv:2607.25628, July 2026) give a kernel-checked Lean 4 formalization of a known/folklore bound (lcm of moduli of any odd covering exceeds 10000), explicitly crediting 'Claude (Anthropic)' with assistance in the formalization's development.

disputes.summary: A separate, unrelated self-published Zenodo cluster by 'Giovanni Esposito' (e.g. https://zenodo.org/records/18440762, 'Global Nonexistence of Odd Distinct Covering Systems', dated 2026-01-31, and several companion papers with titles invoking 'arithmetic renormalization' and 'obstruction energy') also claims a full unconditional resolution. No institutional affiliation, no citations, and no peer review or expert digestion could be found for this author or this body of work; the prose has strong hallmarks of AI-generated pseudo-mathematics applying invented physics-flavored jargon to elementary number theory, consistent with the 'crank flood' of unreadable AI-written preprints described by Thomas Bloom and others in 2026 (see Quanta, 'Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI', Aug 2026). erdosproblems.com does not cite or acknowledge this cluster and continues to list the problem as open. I could not confirm whether this cluster used AI to generate its text (no author statement found either way), so I have not counted it toward ai_role, and it is excluded from the recorded event because it shows no evidence of having been read or verified by any expert (§3, §6.1: a claim with no digestion cannot be even 'claimed'-grade evidence of a change, let alone 'resolved').

summary: Erdős Problem #7 (does a distinct covering system with all-odd moduli exist?) remains open per erdosproblems.com, the authoritative tracker for this exact problem, as of its latest revision. Within the window, the clearest, best-documented event is a May 2026 claimed-and-withdrawn proof: forum user 'jinooklee', working with Harmonic's Aristotle theorem-proving system, submitted a purported proof of nonexistence extending the Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba (BBMST) squarefree-case argument to the general odd case, backed by a Lean 4 formalization that Aristotle's own verification reportedly passed 7/7. Four days later, forum participant Nat Sothanaphan found that a key axiom in the formalization was mathematically false (the sieve-product function as coded is always >1, contradicting the axiom claiming it <1), and the submitter acknowledged the formalization had omitted an initial term from the true BBMST criterion, conceding the axiom was 'provably false'. This is a textbook instance of §6.1's 'instructive failure' clause: an AI-produced/AI-verified claim announced and then withdrawn, coded as status=progress, ai_role=incident, dated to the announcement (2026-05-02) rather than to any resolution, since the problem itself did not move. Separately, I found a self-published Zenodo cluster (7+ papers, January 2026) by an otherwise-unverifiable 'Giovanni Esposito' claiming full unconditional resolution via jargon ('arithmetic renormalization', 'Coverage Fraction βₑ') that does not correspond to any recognized technique for this problem; no expert digestion, citation, or endorsement of this cluster exists anywhere I could find, and erdosproblems.com does not reference it. I treat this cluster as not meeting even the 'claimed' bar (no evidence anyone credible has read it), and record it only as a dispute/credibility note rather than as the driving event — per §6.1, 'claimed' requires a preprint or announcement, but the complete absence of any external engagement, institutional trace, or citation for this specific author across a cluster of grandiose claims is exactly the profile Thomas Bloom (site moderator) and others describe in 2026 as an 'AI slop' flood of unread mathematical papers. I also found a genuinely useful, modest, explicitly-AI-assisted contribution: Mian & Siddique, 'Kernel-Checked Exclusions for the Erdős–Selfridge Odd Covering Problem' (arXiv:2607.25628, posted 2026-07-28), which does not claim to resolve the problem but instead gives a from-scratch Lean 4, kernel-checked formalization of an already-known/folklore numerical bound (lcm of moduli of any odd covering exceeds 10000), explicitly stating in acknowledgements that 'Development was carried out with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic)'. Since this bound was already known/folklore and the paper's own stated contribution is 'epistemic' (a machine-checked certificate) rather than new mathematics, and since the problem is still open, this would fit ai_role=bound / status=progress in isolation, but I have selected the Aristotle incident as the single decisive event per the instruction to describe one event and note others in summary, since the withdrawn claim is the more consequential and more clearly AI-attributable episode in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue the decisive event should instead be the Mian–Siddique Lean formalization (ai_role=bound, since it is a genuine, non-withdrawn, published contribution, whereas the Aristotle claim was retracted) rather than the withdrawn Aristotle claim. I chose the incident because §6.1 explicitly calls out withdrawn AI claims as their own instructive category, and because the Aristotle episode is the more significant test of AI capability on this specific problem (a full nonexistence proof attempt, not just a formalization of an already-known bound). A downstream aggregation pass could reasonably record both if the schema allowed multiple events; I have described both fully so that this loss is recoverable from the summary. Separately, the Esposito Zenodo cluster could in principle be a genuine (if bizarre) human research program rather than AI-generated text; I could not find definitive proof either way (no self-disclosed AI use, but also no verifiable human institutional trace), so I neither counted it as ai_role=generated/assisted nor asserted with certainty that it is AI slop — I flagged the ambiguity in disputes and excluded it from status-bearing evidence because no expert has engaged with it.
what_would_settle_it: For the Aristotle incident: nothing further needed, it is settled as withdrawn/incorrect on the primary forum thread. For the Esposito Zenodo cluster: an author statement (disclosed or denied AI use), an institutional affiliation, or any expert (e.g. a comment on erdosproblems.com or a citing paper) engaging with the claim one way or the other would resolve whether it belongs in this record at all and whether it should be coded as an AI ai_role. For the underlying problem: any future dated, expert-reviewed proof or explicit odd covering system.

corrections.by: hand correction by a human reviewer, not the researching agent and not any automated pass
corrections.why: Nothing qualifying remains once the May 2026 Aristotle claim is set aside — it was withdrawn within four days when Nat Sothanaphan showed the Lean axiom `bbmst_sf_lt_one` was provably false, which the submitter conceded. The record's competing reading proposed re-pointing the status to Mian & Siddique (arXiv:2607.25628), but that does not carry a status either: it is a from-scratch Lean formalization of an ALREADY-KNOWN folklore bound, so no mathematics moved, and 6.2 files a formalization as `none` in any case. The competing reading's suggestion of `bound` for it is wrong for the same reason — a bound that was already known is not a bound moved. Worth keeping in the prose: Aristotle's own verification reportedly passed this formalization 7 of 7 while it contained a provably false axiom, which is the mirror image of the Hopf record, where an AI verifier caught a human error. A withdrawn claim leaves the problem exactly where it was, so it is not treated here as the event the status rests on. Discard it, take the furthest genuine event that remains, and let `status` and `ai_role` both follow that. DEPARTURE FROM THE INSTRUCTIONS, STATED PLAINLY: DEEP_DIVE.md 6.1 directs that an AI claim announced and then withdrawn is recorded as `progress` with `ai_role` `incident`, and the researching agent followed that correctly. This correction overrides it. The instructions are deliberately left unedited, so the record and the document it was produced under now disagree on this point, and this entry is the reason why. The episode itself is not erased: it stays in `summary`, `outcome` and `ai.basis_quote`, and the named system stays in `ai.systems` as evidence rather than as a credit, which is the existing convention for `ai_role: none` records.
